text: Three of the quickest questions you can ask of a table are: what are the biggest items, how do they rank, and how often does each category appear? In SQL those are order by, rank, and group by with count star. pandas has direct answers to all three, and the last one, value underscore counts, is probably the most-typed method in exploratory analysis. We use the illustrative orders table from previous lessons.

Sort underscore values sorts a DataFrame — ascending is the default, so the smallest amount, 45, comes first, and order 5, whose amount is missing, comes last. pandas puts missing values at the end by default, whichever direction you sort — change that with na underscore position equals first. For a descending sort, pass ascending equals False, which pulls the biggest orders, like 310 and 199.99, straight to the top.

Sort by several columns by passing lists — each column can get its own direction, just like order by status ascending, amount descending. Sort by status then amount, with status ascending and amount descending, and you group rows alphabetically by status, with the largest amounts first inside each group. Notice the row labels on the left keep their original values — sorting reorders rows but doesn't renumber the index. Add dot reset underscore index with drop equals True if you want a fresh 0, 1, 2 index.

When all you need is the biggest or smallest few, nlargest and nsmallest say so directly — no need to sort the whole table first. Nlargest of 3 on amount returns orders 4, 7, and 1; nsmallest of 2 returns orders 3 and 8. Both automatically skip missing values.

Rank assigns each row its position in the ordering — the pandas version of SQL's rank function. Rank 1 is the smallest by default, so for biggest-amount-is-rank-1, pass ascending equals False. Order 4, at 310, comes out as rank 1. Missing values get no rank at all — they show up as NaN. Notice ranks come back as floats, like 3.0, because averaging ties can produce halves.

Ties are where the method argument matters. Take a small series with two tens: 10, 10, 20, 30. The default, average, gives 1.5, 1.5, 3, 4 — splitting the tied rank. Min gives 1, 1, 3, 4, like SQL's rank function. Dense gives 1, 1, 2, 3, like dense underscore rank. And first gives 1, 2, 3, 4, breaking ties by row order, like row underscore number. Choose whichever matches how your business actually defines rank.

Value underscore counts builds a frequency table in one line. Orders status dot value underscore counts gives you shipped 5, returned 1, pending 1, and cancelled 1 — sorted automatically from most common to least.

Pass normalize equals True for proportions instead of raw counts — 62.5 percent of these orders shipped. By default, value underscore counts leaves out missing values entirely; pass dropna equals False to count those too. Sort the result alphabetically by category with dot sort underscore index, or turn it into a regular two-column table with dot reset underscore index — just know the column names that produces can differ between pandas versions, so rename explicitly if your code depends on them.

To recap: sort underscore values orders rows, with missing values going last by default. Nlargest and nsmallest give quick top-N lists. Rank assigns positions with a tie-handling method argument, and value underscore counts builds a frequency table in one line. Next: working with dates and times.
